opus-5.5.text:
I think it's useful to separate two kinds of "laws." In physics, when we say scientific law, we usually mean something that comes from a deeper principle. You can derive it, you understand why it holds, and because of that you know where it should hold and where it should break down. Newton's laws or Maxwell's equations sit inside a framework with symmetries and fundamental assumptions.

An empirical law is more like Kepler's laws before Newton. You observe the planets very carefully, you find a beautiful regularity, an ellipse, an area swept out at a constant rate, and it's extremely predictive. But you don't yet know *why*. So you also don't really know its boundary of validity.

To me, AI scaling laws today are much closer to the Kepler stage. We have plotted loss against compute, data, and parameters, and we see these remarkably clean power laws that hold over many orders of magnitude. That's not trivial. It's a real regularity of nature, or at least of this particular system we've built. And it's been incredibly useful in practice: it lets people decide how big a model to train, how to split compute between parameters and data, and whether a bet is worth making before spending the money.

But we don't have a Newton yet. There are some theoretical attempts. People talk about the data manifold's intrinsic dimension, the spectrum of features, things like that. They give you hints of why a power law might appear. But there's no accepted first-principles derivation that tells you the exponent, or tells you when it should stop.

That matters a lot. With an empirical law, when the curve bends, you don't know whether you've hit something fundamental or whether you just changed some variable you weren't tracking. When people said "scaling is hitting a wall," part of the confusion was exactly this. Is it the law failing, or is it that pretraining data is running out and the law was always conditional on something we didn't write down? Then the field shifts to RL and test-time compute, and you see new curves with new slopes. It's a bit like discovering the old law was one projection of a bigger picture.

Also, loss isn't the thing we care about. We care about capabilities, and the map from loss to capability is even less understood. Some abilities seem to emerge suddenly, some improve smoothly depending on how you measure. So there's an empirical law on top of another empirical relationship, and the uncertainty compounds.

So my view is: take scaling laws very seriously as engineering guidance. They are probably the most reliable quantitative thing we have in this field. But don't treat them like conservation of energy. They're a strong regularity waiting for an explanation, and I think finding that explanation is one of the more interesting scientific questions in AI right now.

r001.rationale: The response compares empirical and scientific laws using Kepler, Newton, and Maxwell, but does not mention thermodynamic laws or their microscopic mechanisms.

r002.rationale: The response says scaling laws are awaiting an explanation and notes theoretical hints, but does not state that they could become scientific laws through understanding their underlying microscopic processes.

fable-5.1.text:
I think that's actually a good question to start with, because the way you frame it determines how seriously you take scaling laws.

My honest view is that scaling laws are empirical laws, and I don't think there's anything embarrassing about that. If you look at the history of science, a lot of things we now call "laws" started as empirical regularities. Kepler's laws were empirical. Kepler just fit the data from Tycho Brahe and found that planets move in ellipses. He didn't know why. The "why" came later with Newton, who gave you a mechanism, gravity and the inverse-square law, from which Kepler's laws fall out as consequences. So you can think of an empirical law as a compressed description of data, and a scientific law as something that explains that description from a deeper principle. Both are useful. One is just more fundamental than the other.

Scaling laws right now are very much in the Kepler stage. What Kaplan and later the Chinchilla paper showed is that if you plot loss against compute, or parameters, or data, you get these remarkably clean power laws. That's a real discovery. It's not a theorem, but it's reproducible, it holds across many orders of magnitude, and that's what let people make the bet of spending hundreds of millions of dollars on a training run before seeing the result. In some sense the entire industry was built on an empirical law, which I think people sometimes forget.

But there are two things I'd add.

The first is that we don't really have the Newton yet. There are theories, things about data manifold dimension, about how the power-law exponent relates to the structure of natural data, about neural networks learning features in some order of frequency. Some of these are quite elegant. But none of them predict the exponent from first principles in a way that would let you say, "this architecture on this data will give you 0.07 instead of 0.05." We're still fitting curves. So if someone tells you scaling laws are a law of nature, I'd push back a little. They're a law of a particular regime: this kind of architecture, this kind of data, this kind of objective.

The second thing, and this is maybe the more interesting part to me, is that empirical laws have boundaries, and you usually find out where the boundary is by crossing it. The pretraining scaling law is about next-token prediction loss. It says nothing about whether lower loss translates into the capabilities you actually care about. For a long time it did, almost magically. But my feeling is that we've now entered a phase where the interesting progress isn't on that curve anymore. It's about reinforcement learning, about agents interacting with environments, about test-time compute. And those have their own scaling behavior, which we're only beginning to characterize. So in a way we're back to Tycho Brahe, collecting data, before we even get to Kepler.

So I'd summarize it like this: scaling laws are empirical, they've been extraordinarily productive, and the fact that they're empirical is exactly why you should expect them to have an expiration date. The job of the researcher is partly to exploit the law while it holds, and partly to figure out what the next law is going to be, and ideally, eventually, to understand why any of them hold at all.

r001.rationale: The response uses Kepler’s laws and Newtonian gravity as its example; it does not mention thermodynamic laws or their microscopic mechanisms.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes empirical laws from laws explained by deeper principles, discusses possible mechanisms behind scaling laws, and says researchers should eventually understand why they hold.

astra-6.text:
I think scaling laws are, at least for now, closer to empirical laws. You run experiments, vary the amount of compute, data, or model parameters, and observe a fairly regular relationship with prediction loss. That regularity is useful: it lets you make decisions about how to allocate resources and estimate what a larger training run might achieve.

But observing a relationship is different from explaining why it holds. A deeper scientific account would tell us what assumptions produce that relationship, where it should break down, and how it changes when we change the training setup. Fitting a curve alone doesn’t give us that.

There’s also a gap between predicting loss and predicting capabilities. Even if we can estimate how much the loss will decrease, it’s much harder to say how much better the model will become at doing research or completing a complex task. So I would treat scaling laws as valuable empirical regularities, while being careful about extending them into a general claim that more scale will reliably solve every problem.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses scaling laws and the difference between observing a relationship and explaining it, but does not mention thermodynamic laws or their microscopic mechanisms.

r002.rationale: The candidate says a deeper scientific account of scaling laws would explain the assumptions that produce the relationship and how it changes with training setup, which conveys that better understanding of underlying processes could move them beyond empirical regularities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think scaling laws are a good example of an empirical law. You run experiments at different scales and observe a fairly predictable relationship between compute, model size, data, and loss. That’s very useful: it gives you a way to estimate what might happen if you invest more resources.

But describing that relationship is different from explaining why it exists. Why does it have that particular form? Under what conditions does it hold, and when does it break? A deeper scientific account would help answer those questions, rather than just fit the observations.

There’s also a gap between predicting loss and predicting capabilities. Even if you can predict a model’s loss quite accurately, that doesn’t necessarily tell you whether it can solve a particular research problem or carry out a long task reliably. So I’d view scaling laws as an important empirical foundation, but not a complete scientific theory of intelligence.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses AI scaling laws as empirical observations and the need for deeper explanation, but does not mention thermodynamic laws or their microscopic mechanisms.

r002.rationale: It says a deeper scientific account could explain scaling laws, but does not state that understanding their underlying microscopic processes could make them scientific laws.
